claims.text: The baseline material is a high-entropy alloy optimized for structural performance and lacking an integrated solid-lubricant phase.
Introducing approximately 0.5–2 vol% graphene nanoplatelets by a dispersion technique such as in-situ powder metallurgy can produce a uniform distribution in the HEA.
Uniformly incorporated graphene nanoplatelets will form an interconnected lubricious network in the HEA.
The graphene nanoplatelet network will be located primarily at grain boundaries and within the HEA matrix.
The graphene network will facilitate formation of continuous lubricious films during sliding.
Graphene's layered structure permits facile shear under mechanical load.
Facile shear of graphene will reduce frictional force in the modified HEA.
The graphene network will act as a barrier to direct metal-to-metal contact.
The graphene network will act as a barrier to oxidation.
Suppressing metal-to-metal contact and oxidation will mitigate wear.
Graphene's high thermal conductivity will help maintain the structural integrity of the lubricious layer over a wide temperature range.
The graphene-modified HEA is expected to remain effective from approximately -50 °C to 500 °C if nanoplatelet dispersion and bonding are stable.
Relative to the untreated HEA, graphene addition is predicted to reduce the coefficient of friction by approximately 30–50% under comparable test conditions.
Relative to the untreated HEA, graphene addition is predicted to reduce wear rate by approximately 30–50% under comparable test conditions.
The beneficial effects will diminish above approximately 500 °C because this exceeds the asserted thermal-stability range of the graphene phase.
Nonuniform dispersion of graphene will diminish the beneficial tribological effects.
The magnitude of improvement may depend on graphene volume fraction, nanoplatelet quality, dispersion, and degradation at extreme temperatures.
The long-term stability of the graphene network under cyclic loading is unverified.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in both friction coefficient and wear rate across the stipulated temperature range would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure of graphene to remain well dispersed after testing would falsify the hypothesis.
